list.listitem: The diagnosis of anaphylaxis is made clinically. C
Attend first to airway, breathing, and circulation. C
Epinephrine and oxygen are critical initial interventions. C
Laboratory tests may help confirm a diagnosis of anaphylaxis. Proper timing of studies (ie, serum tryptase) is essential. C

background.definition: Anaphylaxis is a serious allergic reaction that is rapid in onset and may cause death. It is a systemic reaction with varied mechanisms, clinical presentations, and severity.

list.listitem: Fifty to 2000 cases per year depending on diagnostic criteria.
Biphasic reactions occur in 1% to 20% of anaphylactic reactions. Clinically important biphasic reactions are rare.
The incidence of anaphylaxis during anesthesia has been reported to range from 1 in 4000 to 1 in 25,000.
Lifetime prevalence of 0.05% to 2%.
The prevalence appears to be increasing in industrialized countries.
Anaphylaxis is estimated to cause death in 0.65% to 2% of cases.
Hospitalized patients have an increased risk of anaphylaxis.
Patients with asthma are at increased risk for severe symptoms during anaphylaxis.
Food (most common cause of recurrent anaphylaxis).
Drugs (penicillin [PCN] is the most common cause of drug-induced anaphylaxis).
Venoms, especially insect bites and stings.
Immunotherapy injections or oral therapy.
Latex.
Radiocontrast media (causes anaphylactoid reactions).
Exercise.
Acute, generalized reactions.
Type 1 hypersensitivity reactions characterised by release of mediators from mast cells and basophils secondary to the union of IgE antibody and antigen.
Anaphylactoid reactions are non-IgE mediated, with the majority caused by direct histamine release.
Biphasic reactions occur without addtional exposure to antigen.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Atopy (especially for agents administered via mucosal route like food)
Age / Gender (under age 16 more common in men than women, over age 30 more common in women)
Constancy of administration (recurrent administration more likely to precipitate allergies)
Time since previous reaction (less likelihood of recurrence with longer duration between exposure)
Economic status (increased incidence with higher socioeconomic status)
Season (more reactions due to insect stings in summer and early fall)

list.listitem: Avoid drugs with immunologic or biochemical cross-reactivity. C

The previously estimated 10% risk of cross-reactivity between PCN and cephalosporins appears to be overstated. The risk appears highest for first and second generation cephalosporins that have a similar side chain as PCN, therefore consider avoiding cephalexin, cefazolin, cephalothin, and cefadroxil for PCN-allergic patients.
B
Oral administration of possible offending drugs is preferred over parenteral administration when possible. C
The recommended waiting period is 30 minutes after injections and up to 2 hours if drug is given orally. C
Consider appropriate discontinuation of ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers. C
Employ preventive techniques such as pretreatment, graded challenge, and desensitization. C
Skin testing and/or specific IgE blood tests are considered the investigations of choice for evaluation of most potential causes of anaphylaxis. B
Oral peanut immunotherapy appears to be safe and of at least some benefit if tolerated. B
Cutaneous symptoms are the most common manifestation of anaphylaxis. C
Idiopathic anaphylaxis is a diagnosis of exclusion. C
Episodes can present in a biphasic manner. C
Detailed history should be obtained in regard to possible ingestants, preceding bite or sting, and activities (eg, exercise, sexual activity) prior to the event. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Readily identifiable cause; resolves with minimal or no treatment
Drugs, endocrine conditions, and various neoplasms can mimic anaphylaxis
Temporal relationship of ingestion of large gamefish
Consider hemorrhagic, cardiogenic, and septic etiologies
History of recurrent episodes; nonresponsive to standard therapy; found to have complement deficiency; familial
May have history of multiple intubations; unresponsive to standard therapy

list.listitem: See for the diagnostic criteria for anaphylaxis. It should be suspected in any patient presenting with cutaneous symptoms and either respiratory compromise, hypotension, syncope, or other systemic symptoms.
Generally, a clinical diagnosis is sufficient and laboratory confirmation is not necessary.
The level of serum tryptase, a protease specific to mast cells, peaks at 1 hour and remains elevated for approximately 6 hours. A normal level does not exclude a possible anaphylactic reaction.
Clinicians should use caution when using serum tryptase to refute or support a diagnosis of anaphylaxis. The correlation between acute serum tryptase and severity of anaphyaxis is weak.
The beta tryptase subtype may be more specific for anaphylaxis when differentiating it from mastocytosis.

Plasma histamine levels are less useful since levels remain elevated for only 30 to 60 minutes. A 24-hour urinary histamine metabolite (N-methyl-histamine) level is more useful because levels are increased for up to 24 hours.
See for diagnostic criteria and for a treatment algorithm.
Prompt recognition of signs and symptoms of anaphylaxis is crucial. C
Immediately assess airway, breathing, circulation, and adequacy of mentation. C
Epinephrine and oxygen are the most important therapeutic agents administered for anaphylaxis. C
Intramuscular (IM) epinephrine is preferred over subcutaneous administration. C
Massive fluid shifts may occur during anaphylaxis and require aggressive fluid resuscitation. C
Patients who remain hypotensive despite epinephrine should have aggressive fluid resuscitation. C
The evidence for glucocorticoids and H1-antihistamines in the management of anaphylaxis remains uncertain given the lack of rigorous trials. C
Epinephrine is the treatment of choice for anaphylaxis.

Use aqueous epinephrine for acute bronchospasm, hypotension, or systemic reactions: 1:1000 dilution, 0.2 to 0.5 mL IM every 15 minutes for a total of up to 3 doses (0.01 mg/kg in children; maximum dose 0.3 mg). Clinical trials are lacking but are unlikely to be performed at this point.
Use Beta-2 agonist via nebulizer or metered dose inhaler for bronchospasm (typical asthma doses).

Use an H1 antagonist like diphenhydramine for cutaneous reactions or as an adjunct to epinephrine: 25 to 50 mg IM, IV, or orally for adults (1 mg/kg for children, up to 50 mg). Clinical trials are lacking but are unlikely to be performed at this point.
Side effects such as hypotension and reduced conscious level should be considered when using a broad spectrum parenteral H1 antagonist.
H2 blockers can be used as an adjunct, but they are not needed in the acute stages of treatment: ranitidine 1 mg/kg IV or orally for adults (12.5-50 mg for children) infused over 10 to 15 minutes.
It has been reported that treatment with an H1 and H2 antagonist has been more effective than an H1 antagonist alone for the cutaneous mainfestations of anaphylaxis.

Corticosteroids do not work rapidly and are not required, but can be used if the anaphylaxis is expected to be prolonged or to prevent a biphasic reaction. Clinical trials are lacking. Use the oral equivalent to parenteral dosing: prednisone or prednisolone 40 to 60 mg orally or methylprednisolone 125 mg IV (2 mg/kg in children). Also consider corticosteroids for patients with a history of idiopathic anaphylaxis and asthma.
Use IV epinephrine in cardiac arrest and in profoundly hypotensive patients who are not responsive to several injected doses of epinephrine.
Use glucagon for refractory hypotension and bronchospasm in patients receiving beta-blocker therapy (1-5 mg IV in adults; 20-30 mcg/kg in children to a maximum dose of 1 mg).
For persistent hypotension, consider norepinephrine or phenylephrine in addition to epinephrine. Published case reports support the beneficial effect of vasopressin.
Supplemental oxygen and fluid resuscitation should be instituted immediately.
An accidental epinephrine injection is not always an emergency.
Admission is indicated for all cases of severe anaphylaxis or refractory symptoms.
Disposition should be individualized; considering severity and circumstances. There is conflicting literature about the exact time period for observation.
Appropriate follow-up must be individualized.
Recogniton and avoidance are the best strategies.
Clear advice and education should be offered prior to discharge.
Easy access to antihistamines is important.
Patients with severe reactions including respiratory or cardiovascular symptoms should be prescribed injectable epinephrine at discharge.
Educational advice should be gven regarding indications for use, technique and storage of epinephrine auto-injecters.
Management in the elderly does not change; use epinephrine with caution in a patient with cardiovascular disease.
Management in pregnancy does not change; use epinephrine with caution as this may decrease placental blood flow.
Treatment in children is the same as it is in adults, other than differences in dosing noted above in Drug Treatment section.

cell.label: Immediate actions: Establish airway, check vital signs, administer epinephrine, administer oxygen
Readminister epinephrine every 10-15 minutes to 3-5 doses and assess specific problems

Cutaneous symptoms: H1 and H2 antagonist, consider steroids. Wheezing: inhaled albuterol, consider steroids. Hypotensive: fluids and consider vasopressor and steroids. If taking beta-blocker: glucagon and/or atropine and consider steroids
Observe for up to 6 hours depending on circumstances and severity

feature.caption: Clinical Criteria for Diagnosing Anaphylaxis.
feature.feature_body:
Anaphylaxis is highly likely when any one of the following criteria are fulfilled:
Acute onset of an illness (minutes to several hours) with involvement of the skin, mucosal tissue, or both (eg, generalized hives, pruritis or flushing, swollen lips-tongue-uvula) AND AT LEAST ONE OF THE FOLLOWING
Respiratory compromise (eg, dyspnea, wheeze-bronchospasm, stridor, reduced PEF, hypoxemia) Reduced BP or associated symptoms of end-organ dysfunction (eg, hypotonia [collapse], syncope, incontinence)
PEF denotes peak expiratory flow; BP, blood pressure. From Sampson HA, Muñoz-Furlong A, Campbell RL, et al. Second symposium on the definition and management of anaphylaxis: summary report—Second National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease/Food Allergy and Anaphylaxis Network symposium. J Allergy Clin Immunol 2006;117:391-397.
